secs.note: Initial ㅇ has no sound and acts as a placeholder for vowels (아이 = a-i). At the end of a syllable, ㅇ makes the 'ng' sound (강 = gang).
Vertical vowels (ㅏ, ㅓ, ㅣ, ㅑ, ㅕ) go to the right of the consonant (가, 너). Horizontal vowels (ㅗ, ㅜ, ㅡ, ㅛ, ㅠ) go under the consonant (고, 누).

secs.text: Every Korean syllable block has at least one consonant and one vowel: Initial consonant + Vowel (e.g., ㄱ + ㅏ = 가, ㅇ + ㅗ = 오). Many blocks add a final consonant (받침) at the bottom: Initial + Vowel + Final (e.g., ㄱ + ㅏ + ㄴ = 간, ㅂ + ㅏ + ㅂ = 밥).

title.en: The Three Distances of 이, 그, 저

rows: 저 (저 사람 = that person over there)
secs.note: 이 refers to what is close to the speaker. 그 refers to what is close to the listener (or already mentioned in conversation). 저 refers to what is visible but distant from both speaker and listener.

title.en: Spoken Contractions of 이것, 그것, 저것

secs.note: In natural spoken Korean, native speakers almost always use the short forms: 이게 뭐예요? (What is this?), 이건 제 거예요 (This is mine), 이걸로 주세요 (Give me this one).

title.en: Using 이, 그, 저 with Nouns

secs.text: Place 이, 그, or 저 directly before any noun without a particle: 이 책 (this book), 그 영화 (that movie you mentioned), 저 건물 (that building over there). To ask 'which', use 어느: 어느 나라 사람이에요? (Which country are you from?).

title.en: The Three Tenses: Present, Past & Future

rows: Vowel/ㄹ takes -ㄹ 거예요; consonant takes -을 거예요
secs.note: For 하다 verbs: present 해요, past 했어요, future 할 거예요 (e.g., 공부해요 → 공부했어요 → 공부할 거예요).

secs.text: Past indicators: 어제 (yesterday), 지난주 (last week), 작년 (last year), 아까 (earlier). Present indicators: 지금 (now), 오늘 (today), 요즘 (these days). Future indicators: 내일 (tomorrow), 다음 주 (next week), 내년 (next year), 나중에 (later).
